outline.chapter_title: Introduction: The LSTM Legacy and Its Limitations
outline.description: This chapter introduces the historical context of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, their success in various domains, and the three main limitations that motivated the development of xLSTM. It sets the stage for understanding why extending LSTM is worthwhile in the era of Transformers.
subtopics: The vanishing gradient problem in recurrent neural networks
The core LSTM ideas: constant error carousel and gating
Historical successes of LSTMs: text generation, machine translation, reinforcement learning, and more
LSTM's ability to learn abstractions: number neurons, syntax neurons, linguistic neurons, sentiment neurons
Limitation 1: Inability to revise storage decisions (Nearest Neighbor Search problem)
Limitation 2: Limited storage capacities due to scalar cell states (Rare Token Prediction problem)
Limitation 3: Lack of parallelizability due to memory mixing (hidden-hidden connections)
The rise of Transformers and the research question: Can LSTMs compete at scale?

outline.chapter_title: Review of the Original LSTM Architecture
outline.description: This chapter provides a thorough mathematical review of the original LSTM architecture, including its cell state, gates, and update rules. Understanding these fundamentals is essential before introducing the xLSTM modifications.
subtopics: The LSTM memory cell as a central processing and storage unit
Cell state update rule: the constant error carousel (additive update)
Input gate, forget gate, and output gate: roles and sigmoid activations
Cell input and hidden state activation functions (tanh as squashing function)
Complete LSTM forward pass equations
Recurrent weight connections (memory mixing via hidden-hidden connections)
Extension to multiple scalar memory cells with recurrent weight matrices
Ablation studies confirming the importance of all LSTM components

outline.description: This chapter presents the high-level overview of the two main modifications that define xLSTM: exponential gating and novel memory structures. It introduces the two new LSTM variants (sLSTM and mLSTM) and explains how they integrate into the xLSTM architecture.
subtopics: Motivation: overcoming the three LSTM limitations
Innovation 1: Exponential gating with normalization and stabilization
Innovation 2: Modified memory structures (scalar memory for sLSTM, matrix memory for mLSTM)
sLSTM: scalar memory, scalar update, and new memory mixing
mLSTM: matrix memory, covariance update rule, and full parallelizability
Multiple memory cells and multiple heads in sLSTM vs. mLSTM
Integration into residual block backbones to form xLSTM blocks
Residual stacking of xLSTM blocks into xLSTM architectures

outline.chapter_title: sLSTM: Scalar Memory with Exponential Gating
outline.description: This chapter details the sLSTM variant, which retains the scalar memory structure of the original LSTM but introduces exponential gating to enable the revision of storage decisions. It covers the forward pass, normalization, stabilization, and the new memory mixing mechanism.
subtopics: Motivation: empowering LSTMs to revise storage decisions
Exponential activation functions for input and forget gates
The normalizer state: summing products of input and forget gates
Complete sLSTM forward pass equations
Stabilization via the stabilizer state m_t to prevent overflow
Stabilized input and forget gate computations
Proof that stabilization does not change network output or gradients
New memory mixing: multiple memory cells with recurrent connections
Multiple heads in sLSTM: memory mixing within heads but not across heads
The interplay between exponential gating and memory mixing

outline.chapter_title: mLSTM: Matrix Memory with Covariance Updates
outline.description: This chapter details the mLSTM variant, which replaces the scalar memory cell with a matrix memory using a covariance (outer product) update rule. This enables larger storage capacity and full parallelizability. The chapter covers the key-value storage paradigm, the covariance update rule, normalization, and the parallel formulation.
subtopics: Motivation: enhancing storage capacities beyond scalar cell states
From scalar memory c ∈ ℝ to matrix memory C ∈ ℝ^(d×d)
Key-value storage and retrieval paradigm (Transformer terminology)
Bidirectional Associative Memories (BAMs) and the covariance update rule
Optimality of covariance updates for maximal separability of binary vectors
Connection to Fast Weight Programmers
Integrating the covariance update rule into the LSTM framework: forget gate as decay rate, input gate as learning rate
Normalizer state for mLSTM: weighted sum of key vectors
Handling near-zero normalizer values: absolute value with lower bound threshold
Complete mLSTM forward pass equations
Exponential gating in mLSTM and stabilization techniques
Query, key, and value input projections
Parallelization: reformulating the recurrence for parallel computation
Equivalence of multiple heads and multiple cells in mLSTM (no memory mixing)

outline.description: This chapter explains how sLSTM and mLSTM are integrated into residual block architectures and how these blocks are stacked to form complete xLSTM architectures. It covers the design rationale based on Cover's Theorem and the different block types used for sLSTM and mLSTM.
subtopics: Cover's Theorem: non-linear separation in high-dimensional spaces
Block type (i): post up-projection residual block (for sLSTM)
Block type (ii): pre up-projection residual block (for mLSTM)
Rationale for block assignment: sLSTM uses post up-projection, mLSTM uses pre up-projection
Non-linear summarization of the past in high-dimensional space
Pre-LayerNorm residual backbones as used in contemporary LLMs
Residual stacking of xLSTM blocks
Notation: xLSTM[a:b] for ratio of mLSTM to sLSTM blocks
Architecture design considerations and block placement

outline.description: This chapter analyzes the computational and memory complexity of xLSTM networks, comparing them to Transformers and discussing the trade-offs between memory capacity and computational cost. It also covers implementation considerations including parallelization and CUDA optimizations.
subtopics: Linear computation complexity with respect to sequence length (vs. quadratic for Transformers)
Constant memory complexity with respect to sequence length
Compressive memory: suitability for industrial and edge applications
mLSTM matrix memory: no parameters required but computationally expensive
Trade-off between memory capacity and computational complexity
Parallel computation of mLSTM matrix operations on GPUs
Parallelizability comparison: mLSTM (parallelizable) vs. sLSTM (sequential due to memory mixing)
Parallelization analogy to FlashAttention and GLA
CUDA implementation of sLSTM with GPU memory optimizations
Performance comparison: sLSTM CUDA kernel is less than 2x slower than mLSTM

outline.chapter_title: Related Work: Positioning xLSTM in the Landscape
outline.description: This chapter surveys the related work that xLSTM builds upon and competes against, including linear attention methods, state space models, recurrent neural networks, and gating mechanisms. It positions xLSTM relative to the most closely related models.
subtopics: Linear attention methods: Synthesizer, Linformer, Linear Transformer, Performer, SGConv, Hyena
State Space Models: S4, DSS, GSS, S5, BiGS, H3, Mamba
Recurrent Neural Networks: LRUs, HGRN, HGRN2, RWKV
Gating mechanisms across modern architectures: HGRN, HGRN2, GLA, GSS, BiGS, MEGA, RWKV, Mamba
Covariance update rule in other works: Fast Weight Programmers, RWKV-5/6, Retention, Linear Transformer, HGRN2
Most related models: Retention, RWKV, HGRN2 — shared concepts and key differences
The unique advantage of sLSTM: memory mixing enables state tracking
Expressiveness: LSTMs with memory mixing are more expressive than SSMs and Transformers
Residually stacked architectures in deep learning: from ResNets to Transformers to LLMs

outline.chapter_title: Experiments I: Synthetic Tasks and Long Range Arena
outline.description: This chapter presents the synthetic task experiments that validate xLSTM's key innovations: exponential gating with memory mixing for state tracking, matrix memory for associative recall, and long-context processing capabilities.
subtopics: Formal language tasks: testing exponential gating with memory mixing for state tracking
Extended formal language tasks with multi-length training for length extrapolation
Comparison methods: xLSTM variants, Llama, Mamba, RWKV, Retention, Hyena, LSTM, LSTM in blocks
Results: state tracking capability distinguishes RNNs (with memory mixing) from Transformers and SSMs
Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR) task: testing matrix memory capacity
Enhanced MQAR difficulty: up to 256 key-value pairs and context length up to 2048
MQAR results: xLSTM[1:1] performs best among non-Transformer models
Role of sLSTM blocks in leveraging (not diminishing) memory capacity
Extrapolation analysis: xLSTM's enhanced memory allows generalizing to longer contexts
Long Range Arena: assessing long sequence processing across diverse tasks
xLSTM's consistent strong performance on long context problems

outline.chapter_title: Experiments II: Method Comparison and Ablation Studies
outline.description: This chapter presents the comparative evaluation of xLSTM against state-of-the-art Transformers, State Space Models, and RNNs on 15B tokens from SlimPajama, along with detailed ablation studies that trace the contribution of each modification from vanilla LSTM to xLSTM.
subtopics: Training setup: 15B tokens from SlimPajama, auto-regressive setting
Methods compared: GPT-3, Llama, H3, Mamba, RWKV-4/5/6, GLA, HGRN, HGRN2, RetNet, Hyena, xLSTM variants
Model categorization: Transformers, State Space Models, RNNs/linear Transformers
Model size matching: ~350M parameters, embedding dim 1024, 24 residual blocks
Results: xLSTM outperforms all existing methods in validation perplexity
Scaling behavior comparison: xLSTM shows favorable scaling trends
Ablation study methodology: morphing vanilla LSTM into xLSTM step by step
Ablation step 1: integrating LSTM into pre-LayerNorm residual backbones
Ablation step 2: extending to post up-projection block
Ablation step 3: adding exponential gating and matrix memory
Attributing performance improvement: both exponential gating and matrix memory contribute
Gating mechanism ablation: learnable input-dependent gates have incremental positive effects
Individual backbone component ablation studies

outline.chapter_title: Experiments III: xLSTM as a Large Language Model
outline.description: This chapter presents the large-scale language modeling experiments on 300B tokens from SlimPajama, evaluating xLSTM against Llama, Mamba, and RWKV-4 across multiple model sizes. It covers sequence length extrapolation, validation perplexity, downstream tasks, PALOMA benchmark, scaling laws, and inference performance.
subtopics: Large-scale training setup: 300B tokens from SlimPajama, model sizes 125M to 1.3B
Comparison methods: xLSTM, RWKV-4, Llama, Mamba
Sequence length extrapolation: training on 2048, testing up to 16384
Extrapolation results: xLSTM maintains low perplexities for longer contexts
Validation perplexity results across model sizes: xLSTM variants are best
Downstream task evaluation: common sense reasoning tasks
Downstream results: xLSTM best in vast majority of tasks across model sizes
PALOMA language benchmark: 571 text domains ranging from news to Reddit
PALOMA results: xLSTM[1:0] outperforms competitors on 85.1% to 99.8% of domains
Scaling law analysis: power-law behavior and extrapolation to larger models
Scaling law results: xLSTM outperforms Mamba by similar margin as Mamba outperforms Llama
Text generation time: linear scaling of xLSTM vs. quadratic scaling of Transformer
Maximal throughput: xLSTM achieves highest throughput due to constant memory
Batch size advantages: xLSTM can use much higher batch sizes than Llama

outline.description: This chapter discusses the current limitations of xLSTM and outlines future directions for improvement and application. It provides a balanced view of what xLSTM can and cannot currently do, and identifies promising areas for future research.
subtopics: sLSTM parallelization limitation: memory mixing prohibits fast parallel implementation
sLSTM CUDA kernel performance: less than 2x slower than parallel mLSTM
mLSTM CUDA kernel optimization: current implementation ~4x slower than FlashAttention/Mamba scan
Matrix memory computational complexity: d×d matrices are expensive but parameter-free and parallelizable
Forget gate initialization: must be chosen carefully
Matrix memory capacity for very long contexts: potential overload for extended sequences
Empirical evidence: contexts up to 16k do not appear problematic
Incomplete architecture and hyperparameter optimization for larger models
Future potential: impact on reinforcement learning, time series prediction, physical systems modeling

outline.description: This chapter summarizes the key contributions of xLSTM, reflects on the research question posed at the outset, and discusses the broader implications of xLSTM for the field of deep learning and language modeling.
subtopics: Answering the research question: How far do we get scaling LSTMs to billions of parameters?
Key contributions: exponential gating, matrix memory, new memory mixing
Performance summary: xLSTM competes favorably with Transformers and State Space Models
Scaling law implications: larger xLSTM models as serious competitors to Transformer-based LLMs
Broader impact: potential applications beyond language modeling
The enduring legacy of LSTM ideas and their continued evolution
